tekst_en: One more penalty. If Gonzalo Montiel scores it, Argentina are champions of the world.

On the halfway line, their captain waits with his arms around his teammates. He is thirty-five. He has lost four finals with his country, and six years earlier, he said he was finished with the national team. This World Cup final in Qatar is probably his last chance.
As Montiel runs up, the captain looks up at the sky. The same sky he has pointed at after almost every goal, for his grandmother.
Twenty-five years before that night, a doctor in Rosario found that this boy was barely growing. So every night, he pushed a small needle into his own leg.

Almost four years after that final in Qatar, Argentina played in another World Cup final. Two days later, he sat down and wrote a short note. In it were two words in Spanish. Me vacié. I have emptied myself.

He was never a boy who said much. He just played. So how did a quiet boy, who was too small, end up carrying a whole country? It all began on a little pitch in Rosario, on an afternoon when a boys' team was one player short.
In that note, he also thanked his family. Without them, none of his career would have happened. And the first one to believe in him was his grandmother.
It was a little neighbourhood club called Grandoli, in Rosario, in Argentina. The coach, Salvador Aparicio, was looking around for anyone who could play.
On the touchline stood a woman called Celia. She had come to watch her grandson Matías play. And she had brought his little brother too, a boy of four or five.
She pointed at the little one. The coach looked at him and hesitated. The boy was tiny, much smaller than the others. But Celia would not give up. She kept asking the coach to put him in.
In the end, Aparicio agreed. He put the boy on the wing, right next to Celia, and told her: if he cries, take him off.

At first, he hardly touched the ball. But when it came to him again, he took it with his left foot and ran straight past one boy after another. He did not cry. Years later, he remembered scoring twice that day.
In that first game, the other boys were two or three years older than him. Some of them were almost twice his size. It did not seem to matter.
Aparicio never took him off again. And from that day on, it was Celia who took him to every training session and every game.

That boy was Lionel Andrés Messi. He had been born in Rosario on the twenty-fourth of June, 1987, the third son of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother was called Celia too, just like his grandmother. His father worked at a steel factory. His mother worked in a small workshop that made magnets.
He had two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Later, a little sister, María Sol, completed the family.
Rosario is a working city on the Paraná River, with factories, a port, and two football clubs that divide it in half: Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.

The family lived in a simple house in the south of the city, in a neighbourhood called La Bajada. He and his brothers played in the street until it got dark. Lionel was always the smallest of them, and always the one with the ball.

He went to a state school a few streets from home, School Number 66. Many years later, a mural appeared in the neighbourhood with his face on it. The words on it say that he is from another galaxy, and from this neighbourhood.
At home, everyone called him Leo. Later, because he was so small and so quick, his family and his teammates gave him another name. La Pulga. The Flea.
His mother later said that he could be a cheeky, stubborn little boy at home. He hated losing at anything, even at cards. But on the pitch, that stubbornness meant he never gave up on a ball.
His father and his brothers were fans of Newell's Old Boys, the red and black half of the city. On match days, the whole family went to the stadium together. Leo already knew where he wanted to play.
At six, he joined the club his family loved, Newell's Old Boys. In one of his first games, his team won six to nothing, and he scored four.
The boys born in 1987 became a team that people in Rosario still talk about. They called it "La Máquina del '87", the Machine of '87. For years, they almost never lost.
Sometimes the other teams asked for a deal before kick-off: if the score reached six to nothing, the game would simply stop. Even at six to nothing, Lionel was angry if he had not scored himself.

One of his coaches, Carlos Marconi, has told this story many times. He promised Leo an alfajor, a sweet biscuit with chocolate, for every goal. Leo scored so many that Marconi had to change the deal: two alfajores, but only for a header. Soon, the smallest boy on the pitch scored with his head. He turned to Marconi with a smile and held up two fingers.
His teammates from those years remember small things. Before every game, he cleaned his boots carefully and wrapped his own ankles, like a professional. He was eight or nine years old.
One teammate remembers a city derby against Rosario Central. Leo beat the same defender again and again, until the defender's father started shouting from the stands for his son to kick him.
The league kept records of his goals. More than two hundred of them, in five years. People in Rosario say the real number was much higher.
His size was always a problem. Bigger defenders kicked him, and some parents on the touchline shouted at them to stop him any way they could. He got up, every time, and asked for the ball again.
His coaches tried to protect him. They told him to pass the ball earlier, so that he would not get hurt. He kept dribbling. When he lost the ball, he went straight back to win it.
But in 1998, when he was ten, his grandmother Celia died. The person who had brought him to football was gone.

Years later, he said that she had been a very big love for him, and that even today it is hard for him to talk about her. He dedicates his goals to her. After many of them, he looks up and points to the sky.
His mother has said that, after Celia died, the boy would talk to his grandmother and ask her to help him. He did not tell many people. He was not a boy who talked much about what he felt.
Without her, he kept playing. He was still the best player in his team. But something else was wrong, and everyone could see it. While the other boys grew, he did not.
Newell's sent him to a hormone doctor named Diego Schwarzstein. The club wanted to know why its best young player was so much smaller than everyone else.
The tests showed that Lionel's body did not produce enough growth hormone. Without treatment, he would end up ten to fifteen centimetres shorter than he should be.
One word would follow him for years. Small. The best player in his age group in Rosario, and the smallest.
There was a treatment: a small injection, every single night, into his legs. It was very expensive, more than nine hundred dollars every month.
As a boy, he learned to give himself the injections. Every night, the same routine: a needle in his own leg. A teammate remembers seeing him do it before games, as if it were nothing.
A friend's father once taught him to drive, on a quiet country road. Lionel was only eleven.

And every month, his father did the maths. The medicine cost a huge part of what he earned at the factory. The help from his insurance and the club did not last. Without the treatment, his son's football would be over before it really started.
So they looked for a club that would pay. Around that time, Lionel went to Buenos Aires for a trial at River Plate, one of the biggest clubs in the country.
In 2026, Messi told the story himself. He trained there for about ten days, and River wanted him to stay. They even offered to pay for his treatment. But first, Newell's had to release him.
It was the closest he ever came to playing for a big club in his own country.
But when he went back to Newell's to ask for his release, they said no, and the River offer was gone. That ended everything, he said. Then help came from the other side of the ocean.

An Argentinian agent living in Barcelona had been receiving videos of a boy from Rosario. Together with another agent, he showed them to the club, and Barcelona invited the boy for a trial. In September 2000, Lionel and his father flew to Spain. He was thirteen.
At Newell's, his teammates did not know where he had gone. They were told he was ill.
In Barcelona, he played against older boys. The club's sporting director, Carles Rexach, came to watch.
According to one account, the walk from his seat to the pitch should have taken Rexach three or four minutes. It took him fifteen, because he could not stop watching the boy.
One of the boys at that trial was Cesc Fàbregas, who later played with Messi for years. Before the game, a coach told him to mark the new boy from Argentina, and to mark him hard.
Cesc looked at him and thought it would be easy. The boy was tiny. A few seconds later, Fàbregas was on the ground, and the little Argentinian was gone with the ball.

Rexach later said that he told the club: sign him, don't even think about it. But the people above him were not sure. The boy was a foreigner, he was very small, and he needed expensive treatment. The weeks went by, and nobody decided anything.
For Jorge, the waiting was terrible. He had left a safe job at the factory. He was living in a hotel in a foreign city with his son, and he did not know whether they would have a home there or not.
After more than two months of waiting, Jorge called Rexach and said it clearly. If this was not sorted out soon, they were going home.

On the fourteenth of December, 2000, Rexach met the agents at a tennis club in Barcelona. There was no paper on the table, so he took a paper napkin and wrote a promise on it. Barcelona would sign Lionel Messi.
One of the club's directors, Joan Gaspart, later admitted that the napkin had no legal value at all. It was a way to calm a father who was ready to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed it, and the two agents signed as witnesses. Many years later, that napkin was sold at an auction in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
Barcelona agreed to pay for the treatment and to give his father a job. In February 2001, the whole family moved to Spain.
At thirteen, Leo did not really understand what all this meant. He only knew that he would get to play, and that the injections would continue, now paid for by Barcelona.
For the boy from La Bajada, it was a dream. For his family, it was the beginning of the hardest year of their lives.
Nothing went the way they had imagined. Because of the rules for foreign players, Lionel could not play official matches for months. And in only his second game for the youth team, he broke his leg.
His mother, his brothers and his little sister missed home. They could not settle in the new city, and within the first year, they decided to go back to Rosario.
Jorge asked his son if he wanted to go back with them. Lionel said no. Years later, he put it in one sentence: I wanted to keep going, and my dad stayed with me.
So the family split between two continents. Lionel and his father stayed in Barcelona. Part of Jorge's pay covered their life there. The rest went back to Rosario, to his wife and the other children.
Now a thirteen-year-old boy lived eleven thousand kilometres away from his mother, his brothers and his little sister.
On Sundays, there was nobody around. He played video games with his father in the small flat. And then, as his biographer Guillem Balagué tells it, he went to his room and cried into his pillow.
My old man was always by my side, Messi said later, and we went through a lot of ugly things together.
At the club, he barely spoke. In his first training session, the coach asked him what position he played, and he mumbled one word, "forward", and sat down in a corner of the dressing room.
His teammates did not know what to think. Fàbregas later said that for a long time, they thought he could not speak at all. He could. He was just very shy. He did not say much. He just played.
They called him "el enano", the dwarf. But when the ball came to him, nobody laughed.

Slowly, he found his place. His team was full of boys born in 1987, like him: Cesc Fàbregas, Gerard Piqué and others. They played with three defenders and attacked all the time, and people started calling them the Baby Dream Team.

Little by little, the quiet boy began to joke with his teammates. They found out that he was funny, and that he loved cards and video games. He hated losing at them as much as he hated losing at football.
In one season, they hardly lost a game, and Messi scored more than thirty goals. Piqué, who was much taller, looked after him on the pitch.

Their coach, Tito Vilanova, later became one of the most important people in Messi's life. As the story goes, in one game his team was three to nothing up after three minutes. Tito turned to his assistant and joked: what are we going to tell them at half-time, when it is eight to nothing?
Every night, the injections continued. And every year, he grew a little more. By the time he was a teenager, the treatment had done its work.
He would end up about one metre seventy tall. Still one of the smallest players on any pitch. But tall enough.
Many years later, his doctor from Rosario, Diego Schwarzstein, said it plainly: all he did was help a boy grow. Everything else, Messi did himself.

In November 2003, Barcelona played a friendly match in Porto, to open a new stadium. The coach, Frank Rijkaard, sent on a sixteen-year-old from the youth team, Lionel Messi. On the other bench was José Mourinho.
That night was only a friendly. But the boy had now played for the first team. That season, he climbed through four different Barcelona teams, one after another.
His official debut came on the sixteenth of October, 2004, against Espanyol. He came on late in the game, wearing the number thirty. He was seventeen.
At that moment, he was the youngest player Barcelona had ever used in the Spanish league. Other young players broke that record later. He went on to stay at Barcelona for seventeen years.
People at the club remember that he was so shy off the pitch that he hardly said a word. One agent remembered his legs as the thinnest he had ever seen on a footballer.
But one man in the dressing room had already seen what he could do. Ronaldinho was the best player in the world, and he took the quiet boy under his wing.

The other Brazilian players, Deco, Sylvinho and Thiago Motta, looked after the shy teenager too. Ronaldinho sat next to him in the dressing room and invited him to eat at the Brazilians' table. Leo has said that he learned a lot from all of them, but most of all from him.

Not everyone was so kind. A French teammate, Ludovic Giuly, remembered that some of the older players kicked the boy in training, to see what he would do. The boy never complained. He just got up and kept playing.
On the first of May, 2005, against Albacete, Messi came on in the last minutes. Ronaldinho lifted a pass over the defence, and Messi chipped it over the goalkeeper. The referee called offside.
Moments later, Ronaldinho did exactly the same thing again. And Messi did exactly the same thing again. This time, the goal counted.
Ronaldinho bent down, and the boy jumped onto his back. It was his first official goal for Barcelona. Ronaldinho has said he was proud to have been there at the start of that story.

Let me stop the story for a moment. One thing about me. I'm Kamil. I'm twenty-one, and I've been starting YouTube channels since 2014, when I was nine. Most of them went nowhere. A hundred thousand subscribers and the silver play button have been my dream since I was a kid. If this story means something to you, subscribing brings me one step closer. Now, back to the story.

In the spring of 2006, Barcelona reached the Champions League knockouts, and Messi ran rings around Chelsea at Stamford Bridge. Two weeks later, in the return game, his thigh muscle tore, and he left the pitch in tears.
The whole of Camp Nou stood up and applauded him. Rijkaard put an arm around him. Messi was eighteen.
Barcelona went on to win the final in Paris. Messi did not play. He was so upset that he did not join the celebrations. Years later, he said he deeply regretted that night.
Back in 2004, another question had appeared. Messi had lived in Spain since he was thirteen, and Spain's football federation wanted him to play for Spain.

Argentina's youth coaches heard about it and moved quickly. In June 2004, they organised a friendly match for the under-twenty team against Paraguay, mainly so that Messi could play in it and be tied to his country.
Argentina won eight to nothing. Messi has said that playing for Spain was a real possibility. But in his heart, he was from Rosario.

Cesc Fàbregas, his old friend from the academy, has said it would have been phenomenal if Leo had played for Spain. A few years later, Spain won the World Cup without him. Argentina's senior team would wait eleven more years for a trophy.

In 2005, at the Under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands, he was the best player of the whole tournament. He scored six goals, including two penalties in the final against Nigeria. Argentina were world champions.
He also won the Golden Ball and the Golden Boot, as the best player and the top scorer of the tournament. For the first time, the boy from Rosario was a champion in the blue and white shirt.
Six weeks after that, in August 2005, he made his debut for the senior national team, in a friendly in Budapest against Hungary. He came on in the second half.

On his first touch of the ball, a defender grabbed his shirt. Messi pulled his arm away to get free, and the arm hit the defender. The referee showed him a red card. He had been on the pitch for less than a minute. According to reports, he walked off in tears.
Years later, he said what went through his head: I came on, they sent me off, and they will never call me again.
One of his teammates on the pitch that night ran to argue with the referee for him. His name was Lionel Scaloni. Remember that name, because years later, he would come back into this story.
They did call him again. In March 2006, against Croatia, he scored his first goal for Argentina. And that summer, he went to his first World Cup, in Germany.
Against Serbia and Montenegro, he came off the bench and scored the sixth goal in a six to nothing win. At eighteen, he was the youngest Argentinian ever to score at a World Cup.
In that game, he also set up a goal for Hernán Crespo. He was already playing like he belonged.
In the quarter-final against the hosts, Germany, Argentina were leading. Then the coach used his last substitutions on other players, and the game slipped away. Argentina went out on penalties.
Messi stayed on the bench for the whole match. It was the first time a World Cup ended while he could only watch. He said nothing to the press. Again, he did not say much.
In April 2007, in the Spanish Cup semi-final against Getafe, Messi picked up the ball in his own half. He ran past one player, then another, then another, then the goalkeeper, and scored.
He had started on the right, near the halfway line. In about ten seconds, he crossed almost the whole pitch with the ball glued to his left foot.
Everyone in Argentina recognised that goal. It was almost the same goal Diego Maradona, Argentina's greatest hero, had scored against England at the 1986 World Cup. Messi was nineteen.
Barcelona won that game five to two. But in the second leg, Getafe won four to nothing, and Barcelona went out. Even a goal like that could not save his team.
Those were difficult years for Barcelona. Ronaldinho was fading, the team was losing, and the club was looking for a new start. Messi was getting better every month, but he was often injured.
In the note he wrote after the 2026 final, there is another line: I swear I always gave everything. And it was true. But for many years with Argentina, even giving everything was not enough to win.
In the summer of 2007, at the Copa América in Venezuela, Argentina reached the final against Brazil. Messi had just turned twenty. Brazil won three to nothing.
He played the whole ninety minutes and could do almost nothing. In the end, he had to watch Brazil celebrate.
It was his first final with Argentina's senior team. Nobody could have known then that he would lose three more before he won one.

In 2008, he wanted to play at the Olympic Games in Beijing. Barcelona did not want to release him, because the Games were not part of the official football calendar. The case went all the way to a special sports court.
Messi said that the decision was his, and that he would never get another chance to play at the Olympics. The court ruled for the clubs.
But Barcelona had a new coach, Pep Guardiola. He had won Olympic gold in Barcelona in 1992, and he understood. He let Messi go.
At those Games, he scored twice, against the Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.

In the final against Nigeria, in front of about ninety thousand people, his pass put his friend Ángel Di María through, and Di María lifted the ball over the goalkeeper. It was the only goal of the game. Argentina won Olympic gold.

He said later that some things in football happen only once in a life. And it was the only Olympic Games he ever played. He has called that gold one of the wins he values most. And back in Barcelona, Guardiola was about to give him a new role.
Guardiola's first decision was a surprise. He told Ronaldinho, Messi's hero, that he was no longer part of his plans. Barcelona would now be built around a twenty-one-year-old.
Ronaldinho left for Milan that summer. Before he went, he told Leo to take his number ten shirt. The quiet boy who had once jumped on his back now wore his number, and he was the star of the team.
In May 2009, Barcelona went to the Bernabéu to play Real Madrid. According to a book by the journalist Martí Perarnau, the night before, Guardiola called Messi to his office and showed him a video.

Between Real's midfielders and defenders, there was empty space. Guardiola told him to start on the right, and then move into the middle, into that space. And when the ball came, to run straight at the goal.
According to the same book, Guardiola kept the plan a secret until the last moment.
Messi did not play as a winger, and not as a striker. He played somewhere in between, and the defenders had no idea who should follow him. Barcelona won six to two in Madrid. Messi scored twice.
A few days later, in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barcelona were losing in the ninety-third minute. Messi passed the ball to Andrés Iniesta, and Iniesta scored. Barcelona were in the final.
Three weeks later, in Rome, they played Manchester United in the Champions League final. Before the game, Guardiola showed his players a video of their season, with music from the film Gladiator.
Before that final, Leo remembered Paris, the night he had felt left out and stayed away from the celebration. This time, he said, he needed to enjoy it much more.
In the seventieth minute, Xavi crossed the ball into the box. And the smallest player on the pitch rose above the defenders and headed it over the tall goalkeeper, Edwin van der Sar.
Van der Sar was almost two metres tall. Messi was about one metre seventy. The boy who was too small had beaten him in the air.
Barcelona won two to nothing.
That year, they won everything there was to win. The league, the cup, the Champions League, and three more trophies. Six out of six, something no team had done before.
The sixth came in December, in Abu Dhabi, against the Argentinian club Estudiantes. In extra time, Messi scored the winning goal with his chest.
A few weeks earlier, he had won his first Ballon d'Or, the prize for the best player in the world. He was twenty-two. The boy who was too small was now the best.
In January 2011, at the Ballon d'Or ceremony in Zurich, the three finalists all came from the same school, Barcelona's youth academy, La Masia. Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
Most people expected Xavi or Iniesta to win. They had just won the World Cup with Spain, and Iniesta had scored the winning goal in the final. But the winner was Messi, for the second year in a row.
He said he had not expected it. And he said that Xavi and Iniesta deserved it as much as he did, or even more. They were the first to congratulate him.
The three of them gave a press conference together, and they all said the same thing. The prize was for the team.
Years later, Xavi remembered meeting him on a trip: a polite, humble boy, not conceited at all. He said he never imagined that this boy would become the best player in history.

In May 2011, at Wembley, Barcelona beat Manchester United in another Champions League final, and Messi scored with a hard, low shot from outside the box. But the most moving moment came at the end. That spring, doctors had removed a tumour from the liver of their defender, Éric Abidal. Carles Puyol gave Abidal the captain's armband, so that he could be the one to lift the trophy.

In May 2012 came Guardiola's last home game as Barcelona coach. Messi scored all four goals. After the fourth, he ran to the touchline to hug him. Guardiola joked that Leo had stolen the spotlight all season, and that he could not even be jealous.

And in December 2012, he broke a record that had stood for forty years. Gerd Müller had scored eighty-five goals in one calendar year. Messi finished that year with ninety-one, and five of them came in a single Champions League game.

Müller did not sulk. He called Leo a giant, and joked that his only fault was that he did not play for Bayern. A few weeks later, Leo sent him a Barcelona shirt. On it, he had written by hand: my respect and admiration, a hug. Leo himself said that titles mattered more to him than records.

His life outside football had changed too. His girlfriend was Antonela Roccuzzo, a girl from Rosario he had known since they were children. In November 2012, their first son was born. They named him Thiago.
Two months after Thiago was born, Leo said that becoming a father changes you completely. His son, he said, now came before everything else.

In January 2013, he won his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row. Nobody had ever won it four times. But that winter, Tito Vilanova was being treated for cancer again. He was the same coach from his La Masia days, now in charge of the first team. And Abidal had only just come back after a liver transplant. In his speech in Zurich, Leo forgot to thank them. Afterwards, he said he was sorry. Tito, he once said, had believed in him back when Leo was a boy who often sat on the bench.
In Barcelona, he was a god. With his national team, it was a different story.
Argentina had not won a major trophy since 1993, when Messi was six. Now a whole nation expected him to end that wait.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, Argentina's coach was Diego Maradona himself. In the quarter-final in Cape Town, they played Germany. Germany scored in the third minute and won four to nothing. Messi did not score at the whole tournament.
After the game, Maradona told reporters that he had seen Messi crying in the dressing room.
And anyone who says he has no feelings for this shirt, he said, is stupid.

Because that was exactly what many people in Argentina were saying. He had left for Spain at thirteen. He did not play for an Argentinian club. He did not even sing the national anthem before the games.
They had a name for players like him: "pecho frío". A cold chest. Someone who does not feel enough when it matters. To many of them, his silence meant that he did not care.
At the 2011 Copa América, in his own country, fans booed him. His father said that his son was really hurt, and did not understand why they were whistling at him.

The coach at that Copa, Sergio Batista, tried to use him the way Barcelona did. It did not work. Messi said that comparing Argentina with Barcelona was a mistake. Barcelona was a team that had played together for years.
Argentina went out in the quarter-finals, on penalties, against Uruguay. At home, the critics did not stop. So he did what he had always done. He did not say much. He just played.

In April 2014, Tito Vilanova died. He was forty-five. Six days earlier, as Tito's old assistant tells it, Leo had gone to see him at home, and they talked for hours. The coach of his first great team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the World Cup in Brazil, Messi carried his team. After his first goal, against Bosnia, he looked up at the sky, as he so often did. He scored four goals in the group stage. Against Iran, he scored the winner in the ninety-first minute.
He was named player of the match four times. Argentina reached the World Cup final for the first time in twenty-four years.
In the semi-final, they beat the Netherlands on penalties. Their defender, Javier Mascherano, said that without Leo, Argentina would never have got that far.
The final was at the Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro, against Germany again. Messi had chances, and so did his teammates. Nobody scored. Then, in extra time, Mario Götze did.
After the final whistle, Messi was given the Golden Ball, the award for the best player of the tournament. On his way to collect it, he walked right past the World Cup trophy, without looking at it.
He said he did not care about the Golden Ball. The FIFA president at the time, Sepp Blatter, later claimed that Messi kept repeating the same words to himself: the best, but not the champion.
It was his second lost final. Three years later, he said that this defeat would stay with him forever.

In 2015, at the Copa América in Chile, Argentina reached the final again. Against Chile, it was nothing to nothing after a hundred and twenty minutes. Messi scored his penalty. Two of his teammates missed theirs, and Chile won.

Only a month before that final, with Barcelona, he had won the Champions League again, in Berlin, together with Neymar and Luis Suárez. With his club, he won everything. With his country, he kept losing.
The coach of Chile in that final was an Argentinian named Jorge Sampaoli. Two years later, he would become Argentina's coach.
After that final, Messi wrote that there is nothing more painful in football than losing a final. He had now lost three.
In June 2016, there was one more chance. A special Copa América in the United States, a hundred years after the first one. The final was at MetLife Stadium, near New York.
And the opponent was Chile, again. Again, nobody scored. Again, it went to penalties.
Messi took Argentina's first penalty. He leaned back, and the ball flew high over the bar.
Chile won the shoot-out. It was his fourth lost final with Argentina. Three in a row, in three years.
Lucas Biglia's penalty was saved too. But the miss that everyone remembered was the captain's.
A few minutes later, in the tunnel, a reporter stopped him. The quiet man said only a few words: that's it, it's over for me with the national team.
His teammates were in pieces. Sergio Agüero was his closest friend in the team. For years, they had shared a room at almost every camp. Agüero said that the defeat had destroyed Leo.
Messi cried on his shoulder for about twenty-five seconds, like a little boy, and kept repeating the same words: it's not for me, it's not for me.
Later that night, as the team's fitness coach tells it, he found Leo still awake at two in the morning, sobbing.

Then something happened that he did not expect. In Argentina, people started asking him to stay. The president of the country called him, and said in public that Messi was the greatest thing Argentina had. And on a rainy Saturday in Buenos Aires, hundreds of people gathered at the Obelisk with banners. "Don't go, Leo."
Somewhere in Argentina, a fifteen-year-old boy named Enzo Fernández also wrote him a letter, asking him not to go. Six years later, that boy would play next to him in a World Cup final.
The country that had called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later, he announced that he would return. In his first game back, he scored.
He was asked why he came back. He said that he loved his country and this shirt too much, and that he wanted to help.
Later, he explained why he had wanted to leave. It was not only the pain of losing, he said. It was also things outside football that hurt him and his family.
He also said that he was not even sure whether he had told his father before he said it in the tunnel. He simply felt that, in that moment, it had to be that way.

That same summer, a Spanish court found Messi and his father guilty of tax fraud over money from his image rights. Their prison sentences were replaced with fines, as is common in Spain for first offences.
Messi told the court that his father took care of the money. By then, the family had already paid back about five million euros.

In June 2017, Leo married Antonela in Rosario, the city where they grew up. He could have married anywhere in the world, but he chose home. About two hundred and fifty guests came, among them his teammates from Barcelona and Argentina. Thiago and his little brother Mateo sat in the front row, and his brothers and sister signed as his witnesses.

On the pitch, Argentina were in trouble. Before the last qualifying game for the 2018 World Cup, they were not even in a qualifying place. They had to win in Quito, high in the Andes, where they had not won in sixteen years.

That night in Argentina, the streets were almost empty. People watched in bars and at home. In La Plata, the band U2 even delayed their concert, so that their fans could watch the match on big screens. Then, in the first minute, Ecuador scored, and the bars went silent.
And then Messi scored three goals. Argentina won three to one, and they were going to Russia. Even the Ecuador fans applauded him.
In the dressing room, the players sang a song aimed at their critics. Mascherano said that missing the World Cup would have ended the story for many of them.
Messi said afterwards that it would have been madness for Argentina not to be at the World Cup. Now, he said, they had peace.
Their coach, Jorge Sampaoli, said something many people remembered: Messi does not owe Argentina a World Cup. Football owes Messi a World Cup.
Russia did not pay that debt. In the first game, against Iceland, Messi missed a penalty.
The goalkeeper who saved it, Hannes Halldórsson, was also a film director in Iceland. He said he had studied Messi's penalties before the game.
Then Argentina lost three to nothing to Croatia. They beat Nigeria, with a goal from Messi, and he called that win a huge relief.
In the round of sixteen, against France in Kazan, Antonela came with Thiago and Mateo, who wore shirts that said Papá. Argentina lost, four to three. Messi went home again with nothing.

In his farewell note from 2026, he also wrote that leaving the national team was a decision that hurt, and still hurts, deep in his soul. He had felt that pain once before, in Barcelona. And there, the end began on a few nights in Europe that nobody at the club wants to remember.

Things had started to break. In 2018, they beat Roma easily in the first game, and then lost three to nothing in Rome. A year later, it happened again: they beat Liverpool three to nothing at home, and then lost four to nothing in Liverpool.
A few days after Anfield, he said the coach was not to blame. He and his teammates, he said, deserved most of it.
In 2019, he won his sixth Ballon d'Or, more than anyone in history. But it could not fix what was breaking around him.
And in August 2020, in Lisbon, Bayern Munich beat Barcelona eight to two.
Ten days after the defeat in Lisbon, Messi sent the club an official letter. He wanted to leave. Barcelona refused, saying his contract did not allow it.
His father flew to Barcelona to talk to the club. In the end, Messi said he would stay for one more year, because he would never take the club he loved to court.

About six weeks after Lisbon, Barcelona sent away Luis Suárez, one of his closest friends. Leo wrote that Suárez deserved a proper goodbye, and that he did not deserve to be pushed out like that. But nothing surprised him anymore, he wrote.
Then, in November 2020, Diego Maradona died. Argentina mourned for days. The man who had once defended Messi after Cape Town was gone, and the country had still not won a major trophy with Messi.
That year, the world was locked down by the pandemic. And in the summer of 2021, the Copa América was moved to Brazil at the last minute. The final was at the Maracanã, against Brazil.
Because of the pandemic, there were almost no fans in the stadium. One of the biggest games of his life with Argentina would be played in near silence.
The players had been away from their families for weeks. Before the final, in the dressing room, the captain who rarely spoke stood up. Somebody filmed it.
For years, people had said he was too quiet to be a leader. That night, he found his voice.

Forty-five days without seeing our families, boys, he told them. He talked about their goalkeeper, Emiliano Martínez, who had become a father and had not yet held his baby daughter. And he finished: let's go out with confidence and calm, because we're bringing this one home.
Martínez later said that he wanted to cry. Another player said that after a moment, he was already crying, and he did not remember the rest.
In the twenty-second minute, Rodrigo De Paul sent a long pass to Ángel Di María, the same friend Messi had set up for the Olympic gold. Di María lifted the ball over the goalkeeper. One to nothing.
For the next seventy minutes, Brazil attacked, and Argentina held on. Messi had the chance to make it two, and missed. It did not matter.
At the final whistle, Messi fell to his knees and covered his face with his hands. His teammates ran to him and jumped on top of him, until he disappeared under them.
Then he picked up his phone and called his wife and his sons in Rosario. After four lost finals, he had finally won a trophy with Argentina's senior team. He was thirty-four.

After the game, Di María said that the curse had to break one day, and it finally broke. Messi dedicated the title to his family, to the people of Argentina, and to Maradona, who, he said, was surely cheering for them, wherever he was.
One month later, he was supposed to sign a new contract with Barcelona. Instead, the club announced that, because of its debts and Spain's league rules, it could not keep him.
On the eighth of August, 2021, he walked into a room at Camp Nou to say goodbye. Before he could say a word, he started to cry.

He said he was not prepared for this. He and his family had wanted to stay. He had arrived in that city at thirteen, and he was leaving at thirty-four, with three sons, Thiago, Mateo and Ciro, all born there.
He was also sad that he could not say goodbye to the fans in the stadium. Because of the pandemic, he had not seen them for a year and a half.
He signed for Paris Saint-Germain. It never really worked there. When the team lost, the fans booed him.
Once, after a defeat, he flew to Saudi Arabia for a promotional trip without the club's permission. Paris suspended him, and he apologised in a video. By then, everyone knew he would not stay.

In November 2022, Argentina arrived at the World Cup in Qatar unbeaten in thirty-six games. Their coach was Lionel Scaloni, the teammate who had once argued for him in Budapest. Messi was thirty-five. Everyone knew it was probably his last chance.
In the first game, against Saudi Arabia, he scored a penalty. Then the Saudis scored twice in five minutes. Argentina lost two to one. It was one of the biggest shocks in World Cup history.

After the game, Messi came out to talk to the press. There are no excuses, he said. The dressing room was dead. But he asked the people of Argentina to trust the team: we will be more united than ever.
In the next days, the players said that he talked to them more than ever. The quiet captain was now leading out loud.
And a song followed them everywhere. The fans called it Muchachos. The players sang it on the bus and in the dressing room, and Messi sang along.
From then on, every game was a final. Against Mexico, Messi scored first, and Argentina won two to nothing. They beat Poland, then Australia.
Against Australia, he played the one thousandth game of his career, and he scored.
In the quarter-final, against the Netherlands, Argentina led two to nothing, and the Dutch came back to two all in the last seconds. It went to penalties, and Argentina won.

After that game, the world saw a Messi it had never seen. During a television interview, a Dutch player walked past, and Messi turned to him and said, in the language of the streets of Rosario: "What are you looking at, fool?"

The player they had once called cold was on fire. In the semi-final, Argentina beat Croatia three to nothing. Messi scored a penalty, and then he dribbled past one of the best young defenders in the world and set up a goal for Julián Álvarez.
On the eighteenth of December, 2022, Argentina played France in the final. Messi scored a penalty. Di María scored a second.
Two to nothing. Ten minutes left. Four lost finals were behind him, and the trophy was right there.
Then, in less than two minutes, Kylian Mbappé scored twice. Two all.
Extra time. Messi scored again. Three to two. And then Mbappé scored again, from a penalty. Three all.
In the last minute, France had one more chance, but Emiliano Martínez stopped it with his leg. And so, after a hundred and twenty minutes, the World Cup came down to penalties.
Messi scored his. Martínez saved one, and France missed another. And then it was Gonzalo Montiel's turn, with the penalty that could win it all.
This was the moment from the beginning of this film. Montiel walked up to the ball. Messi looked up at the sky, and he said later that he was asking God to end it.
Montiel scored. Lionel Messi fell to his knees on the grass.
He had lost four finals with Argentina. He had said it was over. He had come back. And now, at thirty-five, he was the champion of the world.
Before he lifted the trophy, the Emir of Qatar placed a traditional black robe on his shoulders. And then he raised the cup, kissed it, and did not let go.
Then his family came onto the pitch. His mother hugged him. His three sons ran to him, and he took photos of Antonela holding the trophy.

His goals in the final were his sixth and seventh of the tournament. After the game, he was given the Golden Ball again. The same award he had not cared about eight years earlier, because Argentina had lost. This time, he had the trophy too.
At that World Cup, he became the first player to score in the group stage, the round of sixteen, the quarter-final, the semi-final and the final.
Later, in a TV interview, he said he could hear the cup calling him, as if it said: now you can touch me.
He said he never watched the final again, only the highlights. And that at home, his sons copied the celebrations of their goalkeeper, Emiliano Martínez.
Back in Buenos Aires, millions of people filled the streets. There were so many that the team bus could not move, and the players had to be taken away by helicopter.

In March 2023, before he left Europe, he had one more happy night in Buenos Aires. In Argentina's first home game as world champions, against Panama at the Monumental, he scored the eight hundredth goal of his career. He said he had always dreamed of this moment: celebrating with his own people, at home.

That summer, when his contract in Paris ended, he chose something that surprised everyone. Not Barcelona. Not the huge offer from Saudi Arabia. A young club in the United States called Inter Miami. Many people thought he was going there to slow down.
He explained his choice simply. He wanted to step out of the spotlight a little, and to think more about his family. If it had been about money, he said, he would have gone to Saudi Arabia.
His first game for Miami was in July 2023. He came on in the second half. In the ninety-fourth minute, with the score at one all, he curled a free kick into the top corner.

That first night, he smiled from the bench at Antonela and their three sons in the stands. LeBron James and Serena Williams were in the crowd too. When the free kick went in, the club's co-owner, David Beckham, started to cry.
A few weeks later, Miami won the first trophy in their history. So much for slowing down. And in October, he won his eighth Ballon d'Or.
In Miami, he also became a football dad. All three boys joined the club's academy, and he and Antonela were often seen cheering from the sideline, like any other parents.
In 2024, Argentina reached another Copa América final, against Colombia, in Miami. In the second half, his ankle gave way and he had to come off.

On the bench, he cried. His teammate Leandro Paredes sat next to him. He said he could not even look at him, only hear him cry. Argentina won in extra time without him on the pitch. It was also the last game for his friend Di María.

In September 2025, he played what he said was probably his last World Cup qualifier at home, in Buenos Aires against Venezuela. In the warm-up, he struggled to hold back tears, while more than eighty thousand people chanted his name. He scored twice. Finishing like this, at home, he said, was what he had always dreamed of.
In December 2025, Miami won the MLS Cup for the first time. On the pitch, his son Mateo juggled a ball, and then pointed at his father.
In March 2026, he scored the nine hundredth goal of his career. He was thirty-eight, and some people said he was too old.
It came in a game that Miami did not win, and that knocked them out of a continental cup. The result meant more to him than the record. And there was one more World Cup coming.
His father, Jorge, had always wanted to see him play at one more World Cup. But just before the tournament, Jorge became seriously ill. For the first time, Jorge would not be there to watch him.
In the first game, against Algeria, he scored three goals. Then two against Austria, and one against Jordan. Argentina won their group easily.
And after every game, the same thing. Boots off. Phone out. Was there a message from home? That was how he would know how his father was.
He did not say it then, but he was playing while his father was ill, thousands of kilometres away. And later, he admitted that he never really felt well during the tournament.
In the knockout rounds, every game was a fight. Against Cape Verde, they needed extra time.

Against Egypt, Messi missed a penalty. He did not hang his head. He set up a goal for Cristian Romero, scored the equaliser himself, and Enzo Fernández headed the winner. Against Switzerland, extra time again.
Boots off. Phone out. A message from home?

In the semi-final, in Atlanta, they played England. England scored first. Argentina turned it around in the last five minutes, and in the last minute, Messi crossed the ball for the winner. Two to one. They were in the final again.
When the game ended, Messi was overcome with emotion. Then he walked around the pitch, hugging his teammates and staff. Even his coach, Scaloni, was lost for words.
He had scored eight goals at that World Cup. In his career, nobody had scored more World Cup goals, or played more World Cup games.
The final was on the nineteenth of July, 2026. It was played at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The same ground where, ten years earlier, he had said it was over.
Before the game, in the dressing room, he told his teammates to stay calm, to forget everything else and just think about playing.
Spain had a nineteen-year-old named Lamine Yamal and a team full of young players. They had the ball for most of the match, and almost every chance.
It was still nothing to nothing. In a video published later, Messi can be heard telling his team: character, everyone, character.
At the end of normal time, Enzo Fernández, the boy who once wrote him a letter, was sent off. Ten men, and thirty more minutes to survive.
In the hundred and sixth minute, Ferran Torres scored. Argentina could not answer.
Messi had only one shot in the whole game. It was the fifth final he had lost with Argentina.

After the final whistle, Messi sat on the grass. Yamal came over and hugged him. Messi told him to go his own way, because the future belonged to his generation. Yamal said later that those words meant as much to him as a gold medal.
Scaloni broke down at his press conference and had to leave the room. Before the final, he had said that Messi was the best player who had ever stepped onto a football pitch.
And the next day, Messi wrote to the fans. The pain is immense, he said, and it will take time for this wound to heal.
Less than three weeks after the final, in August 2026, Jorge Messi died in Rosario, after a long illness. He was sixty-eight.
A few days later, Lionel wrote him a letter and shared it with the world. It began with a simple line. I love you, Dad.

He wrote that he had promised his father they would reach the final, so that his father could come and see it. His father never made it. Lionel had wanted to win it, and bring the trophy home to him. But he couldn't, he wrote. His legs had nothing left to give.
And he wrote that during the World Cup, after every game, he waited for a message from his father. When no message came, he understood how bad things really were.
You were my dad, my friend and my agent, he wrote. The same man who had left his job in Rosario, and waited in Barcelona for a napkin.
From then on, when he looked up at the sky, there were two people up there.
On the thirty-first of August, Messi posted the note from the beginning of this film. He had written it on the twenty-first of July, two days after the final, and kept it to himself for six weeks.

In it, he said goodbye to the national team. Me vacié, he wrote. I have emptied myself. I have nothing more to give, and there are great young players coming who deserve their place. Now I will be one more of you.
At the end, he later added one more line: today, after what happened to my dad, I am even more sure of my decision.
He did not write about trophies or finals. He wrote about his family, the fans, and his father.

On the sixth of October, 2026, he played his last game for Argentina, a friendly against Benin, at the Monumental in Buenos Aires. It was River Plate's stadium. The club that had once wanted that small boy from Rosario, and could not have him.
About eighty-five thousand people came. He walked out holding the hands of his three sons. His mother watched from the stands.

The national anthem was sung by a veteran of the Falklands War. Messi could barely hold back his tears. In the tenth minute, the game stopped for a long ovation, and the players of Benin came over to him.
He set up two goals, and then he scored a penalty. It was his one hundred and twenty-sixth goal for Argentina, in his two hundred and eighth game.
His second assist set up a goal for Nico Paz, a twenty-two-year-old, one of the young players he had said deserved their place.
After the game, hundreds of drones lit up the sky above the stadium. And the boy who once sat in silence in the corner of a dressing room took the microphone, in front of eighty-five thousand people.
The first thing he said was that he was thinking of his father. Then he said that this was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks, people had argued about the referees at that World Cup. Messi did not join in. That night, he said that nothing strange had happened. His team had simply given everything they had.

He said that playing for Argentina was the most beautiful thing that could happen to anyone. He would love to be here his whole life, he said. Then he told the fans that he loved them, and that he would miss them.
Then he walked around the pitch with his wife and his three sons, while eighty-five thousand people sang that Messi was not leaving.
He had called it the saddest day of his career. And still, in his note, he had written: I leave with peace, and with pride.
He was too small. He was too expensive. He was a foreigner in Spain and a stranger in Argentina. Later, people said he was too old.
But two people never thought so. A grandmother who told a coach to put him in. And a father who found the money, crossed the ocean with him, and stayed.
He never played only for himself. He played for them. And when he looks up at the sky after a goal, that is who he is looking for.
The cold chest that Argentina once talked about was never cold. He just did not show what he felt. He kept it inside, and he let it out only when he lost, or when he finally won.
And that last final, in July 2026, hurt more than any other. It was not about one more trophy. It was the last thing he wanted to bring home to his father.
Today he is still playing in Miami. He has scored more than nine hundred goals. He no longer plays for Argentina. Now, as he wrote, he is just one more fan.
You might be the quiet one. The one in the corner of the dressing room. The one people think doesn't care.

Leo was that boy too. He never became a loud man. He did not say much. He just played, for the people who believed in him. And when it mattered most, he found his voice. One day, the whole world was listening.
So if you are the quiet one, you do not have to become loud. Keep playing. Your time to speak will come.
And on the night he said goodbye to Argentina, the boy who once barely said a word smiled at eighty-five thousand people. I'm talking more than ever, he said, and I don't want to leave.
That summer, Spain did not only end Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks earlier, in Texas, they had ended the World Cup dream of another boy, who had wanted that trophy just as badly.
A boy from a small island in the Atlantic, whose teammates once called him cry baby. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his full story is right here.
